educational_summary: A warm sub-Neptune (~2.0× Earth) orbiting every ~37.32 days around a Sun-like star (~6089 K) ~2,681 light-years away. Validated from Kepler transits in 2016, it demonstrates how mid-size planets persist at modest flux levels. It’s well suited for discussing mass–radius–density inferences once radial-velocity limits are available.

A companion Neptune-to-sub-Saturn (~7.5× Earth) sharing the system, also on a ~224.78-day orbit in the reported solution. Confirmed from Kepler data, it provides a platform for system-level comparisons—how similar-sized planets around the same star can probe irradiation, eccentricity constraints, and potential dynamical histories.

A warm sub-Neptune (~3.44× Earth) on a ~15.97-day orbit (a≈0.128 AU; low eccentricity) around a slightly evolved, larger-than-Sun star. Confirmed with imaging and spectroscopy, then Doppler (2014), it’s an excellent case for discussing orbital eccentricity constraints, host-star radius effects on transit depth, and comparative planetology with its sibling in the system.

Details for this target were not accessible in the provided record. It likely exists in the archives under KOI/KIC aliases, but parameters were unavailable. This makes a useful teaching example about literature gaps, versioning of public catalogs, and the importance of reproducible identifiers when aggregating multi-source datasets.

A near-Earth-size world (~1.21× Earth) with a ~4.271-day period around a Sun-like star. Discovered by Kepler and validated in 2016, it probes the rocky regime near the radius valley. Frequent transits support precise ephemerides and classroom exercises on transit geometry and stellar-radius systematics.

A hot super-Earth (~1.6× Earth) with a ~1.253-day year ~3,672 light-years away. Discovered via Kepler transits (2016), it typifies USPs at the rocky/mini-Neptune boundary. The intense irradiation and likely tidal locking make it a strong case for discussing radius-valley demographics and mass-loss mechanisms.

A small super-Earth (~1.61× Earth) circling a cool K-dwarf (~4651 K) every ~6.921 days at ~1,843 light-years. Kepler discovered and validated it in 2016. Its shallow yet frequent transits are ideal for illustrating precision photometry, while its size probes the rocky–volatile boundary near the radius valley.

A larger sub-Neptune (~3.9× Earth) with a ~66.42-day year in a system ~3,652 light-years distant. Identified by Kepler transits (2016), it extends Kepler’s reach to cooler, somewhat longer-period worlds. Its size and period enable comparisons of equilibrium temperature, albedo assumptions, and atmospheric retention across the sub-Neptune regime.

A sub-Neptune (~2.2× Earth) orbiting a cool star ~1,169 light-years away every ~11.35 days. Found by Kepler transits and validated in 2016, it typifies the abundant mid-size planets missing from our Solar System. The moderate period provides frequent transits for stacking while keeping irradiation high enough to discuss radius-valley physics and atmospheric escape.

A warm sub-Neptune in a four-planet system, with radius ~3.5× Earth and period ~14.75 days (a≈0.124 AU; low eccentricity). Confirmed with imaging and Doppler work, it’s a textbook example for comparing planets within one system. Students can examine how stellar properties and orbital distance shape equilibrium temperature and potential atmospheric retention.

A compact super-Earth (~1.30× Earth) orbiting every ~2.543 days around a Sun-like star ~3,527 light-years distant. Kepler validation in 2016 makes it a solid example of short-period rocky planets. Its size and period suit comparisons of equilibrium temperatures and potential atmospheric escape timescales.

A super-Earth (~1.46× Earth) on a ~1.435-day orbit around a Sun-like star ~3,061 light-years away. Kepler transit validation (2016) places it among the abundant short-period small planets. Its rapid cadence and shallow transits make it ideal for demonstrating phase folding and signal-to-noise improvement with √N events.

A well-characterized sub-Neptune (~2.27× Earth; ~8.9 Earth masses) in a multi-planet system, completing an orbit every ~16.15 days. Confirmed with imaging and Doppler spectroscopy (2014), it is ideal for lessons on joint photometry-RV validation, impact parameter and limb darkening, and how precise masses constrain interior composition.

A warm sub-Neptune (~2.8× Earth, with sizeable uncertainties) orbiting every ~42.30 days. Kepler validated it in 2016; the sizable error bars make it ideal for teaching parameter inference, stellar-radius uncertainties, and how those propagate into planet radius and density estimates.

Details for this target could not be retrieved from the source record, so parameters are limited. It is likely listed in major archives, but the gap itself is instructive: evolving catalogs, changed identifiers, or removed entries can leave placeholders. Use it to discuss data curation, cross-matching names (KOI/KIC/Gaia), and how scientists confirm or retire candidates.

A warm super-Earth (~1.98× Earth) whipping around a Sun-like star (~6067 K) every ~2.758 days. Validated from Kepler transits in 2016 with low false-positive probability, it exemplifies short-period rocky/mini-Neptune-size planets. Its high irradiation and frequent transits suit discussions of tidal locking and photometric signal stacking.

A sub-Neptune (~2.5× Earth) on a ~41.70-day orbit around a slightly cooler-than-Sun star (~5641 K). Detected and validated by Kepler in 2016, it sits at moderate irradiation where envelope retention is plausible. Its regular transits support equilibrium-temperature and scale-height comparisons across warm mini-Neptunes.

A Neptune-to-sub-Saturn-size world (~7.5× Earth) with a comparatively long ~224.78-day orbit. Confirmed by Kepler (2014), it expands beyond the mission’s typical short-period yield. Its longer period is useful for illustrating survey completeness limits and how fewer transits increase validation difficulty.

A temperate sub-Neptune (~2.35× Earth) on a ~62.89-day orbit ~2,902 light-years away. Detected by Kepler transits and validated in 2016, it helps fill in longer-period small planets within the mission’s sensitivity window. Its cooler irradiation regime is ideal for discussing atmospheric retention and scale heights.

A warm sub-Neptune (~2.58× Earth) with a ~49.10-day year around a Sun-like star (~5518 K) ~3,392 light-years away. Detected by Kepler transits and validated in 2016, it helps bridge the population between rocky super-Earths and Neptune-like worlds. Its longer period within Kepler’s yield shows how survey baselines govern sensitivity to cooler planets.

A warm sub-Neptune (~3.0× Earth) with a ~24.34-day period in a two-planet system ~3,994 light-years away. Validated from Kepler transits (2016), it’s squarely in the populous mid-size class. The multi-planet context invites TTV checks, resonance exploration, and comparative estimates of irradiation among siblings.

A sub-Neptune (~2.9× Earth) in a three-planet system, orbiting every ~5.41 days. Initially a candidate, it was statistically validated (>99% confidence) and remains unlikely to be a false positive. The compact architecture invites lessons on system dynamics, resonance proximity, and how multi-planet contexts reduce false-positive rates.

A close-in super-Earth (~1.43× Earth’s radius) that circles a cool K-dwarf (~4587 K) every ~5.185 days. Discovered by Kepler via the transit method and validated in the May 2016 release, it has a very low false-positive probability. Its short year and small size make it a clean example for teaching transit depth, irradiation-driven atmosphere loss, and why compact, close-in rocky worlds are common in Kepler data.

A near-Earth-size planet (~1.11× Earth) on a ~2.053-day orbit around a hotter-than-Sun star (~6113 K). Kepler discovered and validated it in 2016. Its small size and short period highlight the detectability of USPs and provide a clean case for discussions of tidal locking, irradiation, and the limits of atmosphere survival on hot rocky worlds.

A large warm Neptune/sub-Saturn (~6.6× Earth; ~98 Earth masses) with a ~49.18-day orbit in a binary system; the planets circle the fainter star and have high mutual inclinations. Confirmed via transits and dynamics, it’s superb for discussing S-type planets in binaries, eccentricity excitation, and constraints from long-baseline Kepler photometry.

A temperate sub-Neptune (~2.72× Earth) with a relatively long ~110.97-day year around a cool K-dwarf (~4644 K). Found by Kepler transits (2016), it highlights survey completeness limits for long-period small planets. The cooler host and longer orbit make it a good case for comparing irradiation histories and atmospheric escape thresholds.

A sub-Neptune (~2.6× Earth; ~10 Earth masses) orbiting in ~13.57 days within a four-planet system confirmed with imaging and Doppler (2014). The measured mass allows density estimates, making it a strong case for interior modeling and volatile-envelope fractions. The system context also supports TTV explorations and resonance checks.

A compact sub-Neptune (~2.33× Earth) on a ~13.47-day orbit ~2,703 light-years away. Discovered by Kepler’s transit method and validated in 2016, it exemplifies the dominant class of close-in mid-size planets. The period yields ample events for phase folding, making it useful for classroom exercises on signal-to-noise scaling.

An ultra-short-period super-Earth (~1.46× Earth) zipping around a cool K-dwarf (~4433 K) every ~1.411 days. Kepler detected it via transits; the 2016 validation indicates a very low false-positive chance. Its day-length year invites discussion of tidal locking, intense irradiation, and the detectability of frequent, shallow transits.

A sub-Earth-size USP (~0.61× Earth) completing orbits in just ~0.694 days (~16.7 hours) around a Sun-like star (~5589 K). Validated by Kepler (2016), it’s excellent for lessons on detection of tiny transit depths, extreme irradiation, and how occurrence rates extend into the sub-Earth regime at ultra-short periods.
